questions.q: What are the two parts of DLinear?
options: A moving-average trend and a remainder, each with a linear layer.
An encoder and a decoder with attention.
Subtract the last value of the window from the window.

questions.q: L = 336, H = 96. Weights in DLinear (two [L, H] layers, no bias)?
Which claims are supported by the paper? Select all.
options: A simple linear model was a strong baseline on LTSF data sets.
The tested Transformers often did not improve with longer history.
Transformers can never work for forecasting.
Linear models solve all forecasting tasks.
why: Yes, this is one of their findings.
Too strong; the paper does not claim this.

questions.q: DLinear on a decomposed window: trend = [10, 11, 12], remainder = [1, −1, 0]. A weight matrix maps both to H = 1 with all weights 1 for trend and 0 for remainder. Output?
questions.why: Trend · W_trend = 10 + 11 + 12 = 33. The remainder gets weight 0.

questions.q: A colleague shows a new Transformer with MAE 0.40 on your data. You test DLinear and get 0.39 at 1% of the cost. What do you recommend?
options: Ship the Transformer; it is more modern.
Prefer DLinear for now, and keep watching if the Transformer wins on hard series after more testing.
why: Modern is not a reason when the simple model is as good and cheaper.

questions.q: When is a linear model on the past window likely to fail?
options: Strong interaction effects, like price × promotion.
A clear yearly pattern with lots of history.
why: Linear models can copy seasonal lags.
Trend is easy for linear models.
